item.title: From Bits to Qubits: The Theory and Practice of Quantum Data Encoding
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Surveys quantum data encoding methods across state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM, and block-encoding, synthesizing circuit size, depth, and fault-tolerant gate counts.

Grade 0.484 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Xiao-Ming Zhang, Arthur G. Rattew, Bujiao Wu, Georgios Styliaris, Xiaoming Sun, Bálint Koczor, Xiao Yuan

Figure

Three core access models mapping classical vectors and matrices to quantum operations: quantum state preparation, QRAM, and block-encoding.

Asks

How can deterministic classical data be compiled into quantum representations under minimal circuit depth, gate counts, and non-Clifford resources?

But

Restricted to deterministic, fully known classical data in the standard qubit circuit model with all-to-all or binary-tree connectivity; excludes sampled distributions and continuous variables.

Tools

uniformly controlled rotations (UCR) · Schmidt decomposition · QRAM bucket-brigade architecture · linear combination of unitaries (LCU) · block-encoding

Abstract

Encoding classical data into quantum systems is a foundational step in the execution of nearly all quantum algorithms, and a critical bottleneck in realizing practical quantum advantage. This review provides a comprehensive account of the concepts, algorithms, and practical considerations associated with quantum data encoding. We trace the development from its early conceptual foundations to recent advances, considering commonly used access models, such as quantum state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM and block encoding. We survey the circuit size, depth, space-time tradeoffs, as well as non-Clifford resources required for fault-tolerant implementation. We also discuss the roles of different access models in quantum algorithms. Special attention is given to structured data, such as sparse data, Boolean functions and data represented by tensor networks. This review bridges theory and applications, serving both as a pedagogical guide for newcomers and as a reference for active researchers. We also highlight the pivotal role of quantum data encoding in quantum computing and provide insights into future directions that will enable quantum advantage.

item.title: Experimental realization of quantum-computing-enhanced sensing
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Grover search implemented in a bosonic mode resolves 11 frequency candidates with 2.40 bits of extracted mutual information at m=2 sensing iterations across a Hilbert space exceeding 128 photons.

Grade 0.422 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Yifang Xu, Hongwei Huang, Yilong Zhou, Yunlai Zhu, Chuanlong Ma, Lida Sun, Lintao Xiao, Ziyue Hua, Weiting Wang, Zijie Chen, Weizhou Cai, Hekang Li, Haohua Wang, Xiaoting Wang, Ming Li, Chang-Ling Zou, Luyan Sun

Figure

Measured cavity photon-number populations versus candidate signal frequencies for 1, 2, and 3 Grover iterations, showing extracted mutual information and resolvable candidate frequencies compared to sequential search.

Asks

Can the computational advantage of quantum algorithms be directly converted into an advantage for quantum frequency sensing using an unknown physical signal as an oracle?

Before

Classical sequential search resolves N=3 candidates with 1.58 bits of mutual information for m=2 iterations.

But

Known signal amplitude and duration; non-uniform Fock distribution in initial coherent states causing over- or under-rotation; cavity and qubit dissipation; cavity nonlinearities.

Tools

3D superconducting microwave cavity · transmon qubit sensor/ancilla · signal-driven geometric phase oracle · Grover amplitude amplification · selective number-dependent arbitrary phase (SNAP) gates

Abstract

Quantum algorithms offer computational advantages, yet incorporating them into quantum sensing and converting these advantages into enhanced information acquisition remains challenging. Here, we realize quantum-computing-enhanced sensing in a spin-oscillator architecture, where a microwave cavity provides a high-dimensional quantum register and a coupled superconducting qubit serves as the sensor. The unknown signal directly generates the phase oracle operation, establishing a natural physical interface between quantum computation and sensing. We experimentally demonstrate the first Grover search in a bosonic mode and observe quantum amplitude amplification in a Hilbert space spanning more than 128 photons. For the same number of sensing iterations, our protocol extracts more information and resolves more frequency candidates than classical sequential search. Our results establish signal-driven oracles as a route for harnessing oracle-based quantum algorithms and realizing quantum-computing-enhanced sensing.

item.title: Saving resources through repeat-until-success positive-operator-valued-measure measurements in quantum computation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Multistep repeat-until-success computation guided by intermediate ancillary POVM measurements reduces qubit count and unitary operations polynomially compared to deferred end-of-circuit measurements, achieving total success probability Psucc>12(1+1/e).

Grade 0.421 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Hefeng Wang, Sixia Yu, Hua Xiang

Figure

Quantum circuit schematic for an m-step repeat-until-success POVM computation on n working qubits with one ancillary qubit, showing the repeated unit loop.

Asks

Can intermediate ancillary measurements be leveraged in a multistep state-evolution path to reduce quantum computing resources relative to deferred-measurement circuits?

Before

Deferred measurement requires m control qubits and scales runtime as ∏k=1m1/pk, leading to an exponential decrease in success probability over m steps.

But

Requires state overlap dk=|⟨φ(k−1)|φ(k)⟩| and spectral gap Δ to be polynomially large, with evolution parameter t0=π/(2cd).

Tools

repeat-until-success (RUS) protocol · positive-operator-valued measure (POVM) · quantum resonant transitions (QRTs) · single-ancilla intermediate projective measurement

Abstract

We present a quantum computation approach in which computation is guided by positive-operator-valuedmeasure (POVM) measurements following a given computation path in multisteps. In this approach, one ancillary qubit is coupled to a register of working qubits, and a POVM measurement is implemented effectively on the working qubits by applying a unitary operation on the whole system followed by a projective measurement performed on the ancillary qubit. Each step of the computation is a repeat-until-success procedure such that the desired state of the step is obtained deterministically on the working qubits via POVM measurements. The principle of deferred measurement states that measurements can always be moved from an intermediate stage of a quantum circuit to the end of the circuit without affecting the efficiency of the computation.We demonstrate that in our approach, by introducing intermediate measurements on the ancillary qubit in the computation process, both the number of qubits and unitary operations can be reduced polynomially, compared to the case where the intermediate measurements are deferred to the end of the computation. We also provide a method for implementation of the approach.

item.title: Asymmetric quantum error correction efficiently tackles application-specific noise effects
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Asymmetric (5,3) quantum parity code with 15 physical qubits matches the optimization performance of the symmetric (5,5) code requiring 25 qubits because QAOA objective degrades significantly more under bit flips than phase flips.

Grade 0.416 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Abhishek Yadav, Peter K. Schuhmacher, Michael Epping

Figure

Residual cost deviation Δ plotted against physical error probability p under d=2 layer-level noise for uncoded QAOA and various quantum parity code configurations (n1,n2).

Asks

How do asymmetric bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise channels affect QAOA performance across different circuit decompositions, and can asymmetric quantum error correction exploit this asymmetry?

But

Simulated on a 6-qubit flight-gate assignment problem; syndrome extraction circuit noise and gate-level QEC fault-tolerance overhead not directly modeled in the QEC evaluation.

Tools

Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) · Quantum Parity Code (QPC) · Exact density-matrix simulation · Layer-level and gate-level Pauli noise models

Abstract

Noise is a major challenge for current quantum computers. It can be broadly categorized into bit-flip and phase-flip errors. These two types do not necessarily affect the executed algorithm, thus also the application, in the same way. We illustrate this general effect for the example of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) applied to a small instance of the flight-gate assignment (FGA) problem. We compare bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise under both layer-level and gate-level noise models, using two circuit decompositions of the same ideal QAOA unitary: a CNOT-based decomposition and a native-R_ZZ decomposition. In the simulations, bit-flip noise produces the larger degradation in the performance of the quantum optimization. The asymmetry is most visible in the layer-level and native-R_ZZ simulations. We explain this by how the errors affect mixing, final measurements, and how they propagate inside the circuit. We then exploit these insights to tackle noise particularly efficiently using asymmetric error-correcting codes. As an illustration, we use the quantum parity code (QPC), a generalization of the 9-qubit Shor code, and show that a smaller asymmetric code can achieve nearly the same improvement as a larger symmetric choice. This demonstrates that error-correction resources should be assigned not only according to physical error rates, but also according to how strongly each error channel affects the application. As a result, asymmetric quantum error correction proves useful even in cases where the noise model is symmetric. Finally, we discuss how information about the noise obtained through calibration can be exploited in our approach.

item.title: Near-optimal synthesis of non-Gaussian phase gates via qubit-oscillator Rabi control
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Analytic Rabi sequence approximates degree-R continuous-variable polynomial phase gates eiTp(Xˆ) over Fock subspace ℋn with total interaction time Ttot=O(log(R−1)/2+o(1)⁡(1/ε)), matching the proven lower bound Ω(log(R−1)/2⁡(1/ε)).

Grade 0.412 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Zhen Yang, Shan Jin, Zi-Wen Liu, Xiaoting Wang

Figure

Approximation error as a function of total Rabi interaction time Ttot for representative continuous-variable phase evolutions.

Asks

Can continuous-variable non-Gaussian polynomial phase gates be synthesized via linear qubit-oscillator Rabi control with polylogarithmic total interaction time in the inverse target error 1/ε?

Before

Fourier-Trotter approaches require sequence length O(1/ε) to achieve target error ε.

But

Applies to input states within fixed finite Fock subspace ℋn=span⁡{|0⟩,…,|n⟩}; exact synthesis is impossible for finite same-quadrature Rabi sequences.

Tools

generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP) · qubit-oscillator linear Rabi coupling · qubit postselection · polarization decomposition

Abstract

Non-Gaussian gates remain a key bottleneck for universal continuous-variable (CV) quantum computation because the nonlinearities they require are difficult to engineer. To address this challenge, we develop an efficient qubit-oscillator Rabi synthesis scheme for polynomial phase gates, with a total interaction time that scales polylogarithmically with the inverse target error \(ε\). Specifically, for a class of readily preparable initial states, we show that a degree-\(R\) phase gate can be approximated by an analytically constructed Rabi sequence with total time \(O(log^(R-1)/2+o(1)(1/ε))\). This construction requires no numerical optimization and therefore extends naturally to arbitrarily large multimode systems. We further establish a total-time lower bound of \(Ω(log^(R-1)/2(1/ε))\), showing that the synthesis is near optimal. As applications, we use this scheme to simulate representative CV quantum dynamics and implement a CV quantum algorithm for solving linear partial differential equations. These results establish qubit-oscillator Rabi control as an efficient, analytically compilable, and near-optimal primitive for CV quantum information processing.

item.title: Wavelength-Uniform Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Dynamics
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Constructed an end-to-end quantum algorithm for the von Neumann equation with polynomial complexity in dimension d and resource bounds containing no negative powers of the semiclassical parameter ε. Evaluated physical observables uniformly across ε∈[10−4,1] with observable error Eobs≤6.8126×10−7 under fixed grid parameters.

Grade 0.402 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “A variational eigenvalue solver on a photonic quantum processor” · Shi Jin, Chuwen Ma

Figure

Observable error Eobs as a function of grid refinement parameters and across nine values of ε from 10−4 to 1, demonstrating ε-uniform convergence below the 10−5 tolerance with fixed (M,K,Q)=(256,36,16).

Asks

How can quantum dynamics in the semiclassical regime ε≪1 be simulated on a quantum computer without spatial mesh and query constraints scaling inversely with ε?

Before

Standard spatial spectral methods and wave-function representations require spatial mesh h=O(ε) and O(ε−d) spatial unknowns due to the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem; Gaussian wave-packet methods require h=O(ε) and cost O(ε−d/2) per step.

But

Applies to smooth physical observables (pairing with Lx,y2 windows) rather than full density matrix state reconstruction; requires uniform regularity of the density operator in Weyl variables.

Tools

Weyl variables · Hermite-Galerkin projection · Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) · Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU) · Qubitized Hamiltonian simulation

Abstract

One of the main challenges in quantum simulation is the prohibitive cost of computing its solutions in the semi-classical regime, in which the de Broglie wavelength is small compared with the characteristic length scale and the solution is highly oscillatory. This difficulty is overcome by using the Weyl variable, under which the solution is not oscillatory. Furthermore, we use the exact Hermite moments and quantum singular value transformation to treat the polynomial and Fourier components of the potential, resulting in a quantum algorithm efficient for all ranges of wavelengths. Specifically, it has a polynomial complexity in spatial dimension, and discretization and query bounds without negative powers of possibly small wavelength, thus enabling it to capture the correct physical observables even if the spatial grid does not resolve the frequency, hence defying the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem.

item.title: Reducing quantum and classical resources for quantum-centric supercomputing workloads on near-term hardware
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Approximate compilation reduces the largest 40-qubit Krylov circuit depth from 2413 to 26 and two-qubit gates from 6840 to 74 with 0.941 fidelity, overcoming depolarizing noise stagnation to restore monotonic ground-state energy convergence in Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization.

Grade 0.400 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Maxence Grandadam, Vladyslav Bohun, Dikshant Dulal, Maciej Koch-Janusz

Figure

Energy error ΔE (top) and classical subspace dimension (bottom) plotted against Krylov dimension d. Uncompressed circuits stagnate near ΔE≈9×10−2t, while compressed circuits achieve monotonic convergence with smaller classical subspaces.

Asks

How does hardware noise affect sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization support recovery, and can approximate circuit compilation mitigate the resulting exponential depth penalty?

Before

Uncompressed Qiskit circuits stagnate at an energy error ΔE≈9×10−2t due to noise accumulation across increasing Krylov depth.

But

One-dimensional single-impurity Anderson model with bounded entanglement allowing single-block Trotter compression, evaluated on 20 sites (40 qubits) with 1000 shots per state.

Tools

Sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SKQD) · Tensor-network approximate circuit compilation · ibm_fez superconducting quantum processor · Single-impurity Anderson model (SIAM)

Abstract

Sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SKQD) is a paradigmatic example of a quantum-centric supercomputing workflow that combines the convergence structure of Krylov quantum diagonalization with classical sampling-based post-processing. It provides convergence guarantees assuming that the important computational-basis configurations can be sampled from a set of Krylov states with sufficient probability. We analyze this assumption under depolarizing noise, deriving shot-count resource estimates that expose an exponential depth penalty, and perform experiments on current noisy hardware with the one-dimensional single-impurity Anderson model on a 20-site (40-qubit) instance. Device noise breaks the practical convergence predicted by the noiseless SKQD analysis, but approximate compilation techniques can compress the Krylov time-evolution circuits before execution. The compressed circuits accumulate less hardware noise, recover the expected energy convergence, and reduce both the quantum shot budget and the classical subspace dimension, remaining beneficial even when classical configuration recovery is applied.

item.title: From NISQ to Fault-Tolerance: Applications and Algorithmic Benchmarks for Spin Qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Compiling Parity Twine to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits reduces the physical exchange-pulse count by more than 22% for QFT and up to 34% for QAOA compared to baseline compilation schemes.

Grade 0.395 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Frederik Lohof, Florian Ginzel, Wolfgang Lechner

Figure

Physical exchange-pulse count and Twine/Fowler pulse count ratio as a function of device length L for the quantum Fourier transform.

Asks

How do algorithmic benchmarks and simulation routines scale from NISQ to fault-tolerance when mapped directly to physical exchange-pulse sequences on exchange-only spin qubit QPUs?

But

Analytical and numerical compilation models; assumes single-pulse error rates p≈1.5×10−4, readout error pm≈0.01, and T2≈19.3 μs.

Tools

Parity Twine compilation · exchange-only (EO) spin qubits · pulse-level scheduling with exclusion radius · surface code QEC / lattice surgery error modeling

Abstract

Motivated by recent breakthroughs in the development of spin-based quantum processing units based on exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, we provide a roadmap for the implementation of quantum algorithms on the EO platform, ranging from the NISQ to the fault-tolerant era. To provide an algorithm-driven perspective on the scaling of quantum chips, we consider a range of applications targeting different stages of hardware maturity and formulate requirements for a successful realization. We show that the compilation method Parity Twine perfectly complements the hardware's capabilities to perform tasks such as the quantum Fourier transform or QAOA. Furthermore, we describe an error detection technique native to Parity Twine, which EO qubits can leverage in a unique and advantageous way to improve algorithm performance. Finally, since both near-term algorithmic benchmarks and a long-term perspective can be found in digital quantum simulation, we specifically discuss the fermionic fast Fourier transform and the simulation of Fermi-Hubbard models. The latter is explicitly discussed in the context of quantum error correction and a partially fault-tolerant realization. By providing detailed resource estimates and identifying scaling bottlenecks on each level, our work offers a quantitative perspective on EO-based quantum computing and will inform future hardware design choices.
